interactive.title: The system curve builder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This short lesson runs over fifteen small screens. The main picture is a pump lifting seawater from a low tank to a high one through a pipe. The lift is the height between the two water surfaces. A lift slider sets it from 0 to 20 m, in steps of 1, starting at 10 m. A length slider sets the pipe's length from 10 to 150 m, in steps of 10, starting at 70 m. A bore stepper picks the pipe's inside diameter: 50, 65, 80 or 100 mm. It starts at 65 mm. A flow slider runs from 0 to 12 L/s in steps of 0.5, starting at 10 L/s. Dots ride along the pipe at the water's speed. That speed is the flow ÷ the bore's area. At the start it is 0.01 m³/s ÷ 0.00332 m², about 3.0 m/s. Two stacked bars stand beside the pump, in metres of seawater. The lower bar is the lift. It stays the same at every flow, because it depends only on the two surfaces. The upper bar is the friction head, worked out as f × (L ÷ D) × v² ÷ 2g. L is the pipe's length and D its bore, both in metres. v is the water's speed, and g is 9.81. f is a friction factor, held at 0.02 throughout. Because v is squared, twice the flow makes the friction bar four times as tall. At the start the friction is about 10.0 m, so the total head is about 20.0 m. A graph beside the bars plots head up the side against flow along the bottom. Each flow you set drops a dot at its total head. The dots trace the system curve. It starts at the lift at zero flow, then bends upward as the flow squared. The head axis stretches to fit the tallest dot. A chain runs below. Its first link is the hydraulic power, ρ × g × Q × H. ρ is seawater's density, 1025 kg/m³. Q is the flow in m³/s, and H is the total head. At the start that is 1025 × 9.81 × 0.01 × 20.0, about 2.01 kW. The next link is the shaft power, the hydraulic power ÷ the pump's efficiency. Taking that efficiency as 70% gives about 2.87 kW. The next is the motor's input, the shaft power ÷ the motor's efficiency. Taking that as 90% gives about 3.19 kW. The chain ends on an ammeter. The motor runs on 440 V three-phase, with a power factor taken as 0.85. Its line current is the input ÷ (√3 × 440 × 0.85), about 4.9 A. Three readouts show the total head, the hydraulic power and the motor's current. On a phone they wrap onto two rows. Screen by screen, it runs like this. Screen 1 shows a gauge on a seawater tank reading 100 kPa. Beside it stands the column of seawater that pressure holds up. The column is about 9.9 m tall, since 100,000 ÷ (1025 × 9.81) is about 9.9. The open tube is a simple manometer. Screen 2 shows two gauges on the same rising pressure. In a U-tube manometer the liquid falls in one leg and rises in the other, and the gap between the levels is the head. In a Bourdon gauge a C-shaped tube straightens a little and turns the needle. Screen 3 asks a question. A pump moves seawater, and its outlet gauge reads 200 kPa more than its inlet gauge. What head is that? Is it about 19.9 m, about 20.4 m or about 195 m? Screen 4 shows the pump and tanks with the flow at 0. Only the lift bar stands, at 10 m. It moves with the lift slider. Screen 5 asks for a prediction before the friction bar appears. The flow through the same pipe doubles. What happens to the friction head? Does it double, grow four times as big, or stay the same? Screen 6 adds the friction bar on top of the lift bar, and the flow slider runs it. At 5 L/s the friction is about 2.5 m. At 10 L/s it is about 10.0 m, four times as much. Screen 7 works Darcy's rule a factor at a time for 50 m of 50 mm pipe at 2 m/s. f is 0.02, L ÷ D is 1000, and v² ÷ 2g is 2² ÷ 19.62, about 0.204. Their product is about 4.1 m. Screen 8 asks a question. 50 m of 50 mm pipe loses about 4.1 m at 2 m/s. How much does 150 m of the same pipe lose at the same speed? Is it about 12.2 m, about 36.7 m or about 4.1 m? Screen 9 sweeps the flow from 0 to 12 L/s. The dots it drops trace the system curve. Moving the lift slider then shifts the whole curve up or down without changing its shape. A longer pipe or a smaller bore makes it bend up more steeply. So a system that is mostly lift has a flat curve, and one that is mostly friction has a steep one. Screen 10 asks a question. A system has a lift of 10 m and loses 4 m to friction at 5 L/s. What head does it need at 10 L/s? Is it 26 m, 18 m or 56 m? Screen 11 lights the chain link by link at 10 L/s and 20.0 m. It reads about 2.01 kW, then 2.87 kW, then 3.19 kW. Screen 12 asks a question. The hydraulic power is 2.01 kW and the pump's efficiency is 70%. What power must the shaft give? Is it about 2.87 kW, about 1.41 kW or about 2.01 kW? Screen 13 shows the ammeter at about 4.9 A. Raising the flow from 10 to 12 L/s takes it to about 7.2 A, because both the flow and the head have grown. Screens 14 and 15 bring it all together. Screen 14 has a pump sending 5 L/s of seawater up a lift of 12 m. The pipe loses 3 m to friction, and the pump's efficiency is 75%. What power must the shaft give? Is it about 1.01 kW, about 0.57 kW or about 0.80 kW? The head is 12 + 3 = 15 m. So the hydraulic power is 1025 × 9.81 × 0.005 × 15, about 754 W. That ÷ 0.75 is about 1.01 kW. Screen 15 keeps the same flow through the same length of pipe, but replaces a 100 mm bore with a 50 mm one. How many times the friction head does that give? Is it about 32 times, 4 times or 16 times? Half the bore has a quarter of the area, so the water goes four times as fast. That squared is 16. L ÷ D also doubles, so the friction grows 32 times. On the picture, at 70 m and 10 L/s, about 1.16 m becomes about 37.0 m. Where it can, the picture draws a wrong pick, so you see where it fails.
interactive.ignores: Here you set the flow yourself, as if the pump gave whatever flow you asked for. A real pump settles at one flow, where its own curve crosses this one. Finding that crossing is the next step. The friction factor is held at 0.02. A real one depends on the pipe's roughness and changes a little with speed. So friction grows close to the flow squared, not exactly. At very low flows water can run in smooth layers. There friction grows only in step with the speed, but the model uses the eddying rule at every flow. The pipe is drawn straight, but bends, valves and fittings add more loss. The tanks' levels are held still while you pump. The model leaves out the small head the water still carries as it leaves the pipe's end. The efficiencies and the power factor are held fixed, though real ones change with the load. The speed is drawn the same across the pipe. Real water moves faster in the middle than at the walls.

explain.text:
A pump has to give the water two things. It must lift it from one surface to the other. It must also push it through the pipe against friction. Both are measured as a height of liquid, called head. The friction part grows with the flow squared. Head × flow then sets the power the pump needs, and so the current its motor draws.

Start from pressure in a liquid. A column of seawater h metres tall presses ρgh on its base. Turn that round, and any pressure reads as a height: h = p ÷ ρg. Seawater's density is 1025 kg/m³.[^1] So 100 kPa holds up 100,000 ÷ (1025 × 9.81), about 9.9 m of it. That height is [[head]]. A pump's head is the height it can raise the liquid, in metres.[^3] Head is also energy. Lifting a weight of 1 N through 1 m takes 1 J. So each metre of head gives 1 J to every newton of liquid.

An open tube rising from a tank shows that height directly. It is the simplest [[manometer]]. A U-tube manometer is a bent tube, part-filled with liquid. One leg joins the pipe, and the other is open to the air. The gap between the two levels is the pressure, as a head of that liquid.[^7] A [[Bourdon gauge]] hides a flattened tube, bent into a C. Pressure makes it straighten a little, and its tip turns the needle.[^8] It reads gauge pressure, the pressure above the air around it.[^9]

With both tanks open to the air, the head a pipe needs has two parts. The lift is the height between the two water surfaces. While the tanks' levels hold, the lift is the same at any flow, even none. The friction head is the energy lost on the way. It depends on the pipe's length and size, and on its bends and valves.[^4] In eddying flow it grows with the square of the water's speed.[^5] Here is one way to picture why. Moving water carries ½ρv² of kinetic energy in every cubic metre. Over each stretch of pipe, the eddies turn a share of it into heat. Twice the speed carries four times the energy, so four times as much is lost.

Darcy's rule puts it in numbers: friction head = f × (L ÷ D) × v² ÷ 2g. L is the length and D the bore, both in metres. f is a friction factor. It is set mostly by how rough the pipe is for its bore. Say f is 0.02. Then 50 m of 50 mm pipe at 2 m/s loses 0.02 × 1000 × 2² ÷ 19.62, about 4.1 m. At 4 m/s it loses about 16.3 m. Twice the speed loses four times the head, not twice. Add the lift and the friction at every flow, and you get the [[system curve]]. It starts at the lift and bends upward as the flow squared. This is a simplified model. Real pipes add bends and valves, and a real f shifts a little with speed. If the far tank is under pressure, that pressure ÷ ρg adds to the lift.

Now the power. Each second the pump moves Q cubic metres of water, which weigh ρgQ newtons. It raises each newton through H metres of head. So the power it gives the water is ρgQH watts. That is the [[hydraulic power]]. Seawater at 10 L/s against 20 m of head takes 1025 × 9.81 × 0.01 × 20, about 2.01 kW. The pump wastes some of what its shaft gives it, so the shaft must give more. At 70% efficiency that is 2.01 ÷ 0.7, about 2.87 kW.[^2] The motor wastes some too, so it draws more again from the supply.[^6] At 90% that is about 3.19 kW. Each efficiency divides, because each stage takes in more than it passes on. On 440 V three-phase at a power factor of 0.85, the ammeter reads about 4.9 A.

**A pipe needs head for its lift plus friction that grows with the flow squared. That head × the flow sets the pump's power and its motor's current.**

analogy.text: Think of charging a battery through long leads. Before any current flows, the charger must match the battery's own voltage. That is the lift. Then it must add the drop in the leads, which grows with the current. That is the friction. The charger's power is its voltage × the current, just as the pump's is head × flow. The share that matches the battery goes into storage, just as the lift stores energy in the high tank. The drop in the leads is lost as heat, just as friction is.
analogy.breaks: By Ohm's law, the leads' drop grows in step with the current. Pipe friction grows with the flow squared. Size matters far more in a pipe too. Halve a lead's diameter, and its drop at the same current goes up four times. Halve a pipe's bore, and its friction at the same flow goes up about 32 times.

practice.text:
**Safe first:** Isolate and lock off a pump's motor before you work on the pump. Isolate and vent its pipework too, as for any pipe under pressure.

**Working out the power a pump needs**
- Find the lift: the height between the two water surfaces, in metres. If the far end is under pressure, add that pressure ÷ ρg.
- Find the speed: the flow in m³/s ÷ the bore's area in m².
- Friction head = f × (L ÷ D) × v² ÷ 2g, with L and D both in metres. Add the loss in bends and valves where you know it.
- Total head H = lift + friction head.
- Hydraulic power = ρ × g × Q × H, in watts, with Q in m³/s.
- Shaft power = hydraulic power ÷ the pump's efficiency.
- Motor input = shaft power ÷ the motor's efficiency.
- Line current = motor input ÷ (√3 × line voltage × power factor).

**Rules of thumb:** About 10 kPa of seawater pressure is 1 m of head. Twice the flow needs about four times the friction head. At the same flow, half the bore gives about 32 times the friction. A system that is mostly lift needs much the same head at any flow. A system that is mostly friction needs far more head as the flow climbs.

**Worked example:** A pump lifts seawater at 10 L/s against 20 m of head. That flow is 0.01 m³/s. The hydraulic power is 1025 × 9.81 × 0.01 × 20, about 2.01 kW. With the pump at 70%, the shaft must give about 2.87 kW. With the motor at 90%, it draws about 3.19 kW. On 440 V three-phase at a power factor of 0.85, the line current is 3,190 ÷ (1.732 × 440 × 0.85), about 4.9 A. Pump makers often work in m³/h, which gives a quick check: kW = Q × H × relative density ÷ (367.46 × efficiency).[^2] 10 L/s is 36 m³/h. So 36 × 20 × 1.025 ÷ (367.46 × 0.7) gives about 2.87 kW again.

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying by an efficiency instead of dividing. The motor takes in more than the shaft gives out.
- Treating friction as growing in step with the flow. In eddying flow it grows with the flow squared.
- Reading a pressure as head without dividing by ρg.
- Leaving the flow in L/s, or the bore in mm.
- Forgetting the lift, or counting friction when nothing flows.

applied.problem: "The head a pipe needs has two parts" holds only when both ends are open to the same air; pumping into a pressurised tank or overboard against sea pressure adds that pressure ÷ ρg to the lift. Also f depends on roughness relative to the bore, not roughness alone.

The job steps take the lift as surface height alone, which undercounts the head whenever the delivery end is under pressure, such as a pressurised tank or discharge overboard at depth; the step must add that pressure ÷ ρg.
